newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian business welcomes release of funds.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian business welcomes release of funds.

text.p: Nigeria's business community on Tuesday welcomed reports that the military government had released long-awaited funds to its ministries.
But it cautioned that in the long term the economy would be healthier if the ruling generals were to revitalise utilities and stimulate growth through privatisation.
"It is better late than never and even at this late stage of the year it can revitalise sectors that are virtually dead," Uzor Okeke of the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria told Reuters.
The News Agency of Nigeria on Monday said the finance ministry had released 32.8 billion naira ($397.6 million), from the 89 billion naira ($1,072 million) budgeted for capital projects in 1997.
"They haven't told us officially, but we are pretty certain that that is what is behind an increase in liquidity at the tail end of last week," said one banker in the commercial capital Lagos.
It is not yet clear which ministries have received money.

Bankers said that a further increase of liquidity was likely as more ministries and state-run bodies sought to put their money into action over coming days, and cautioned that it was likely to mean higher inflation.
Low inflation and a stable naira currency are policy goals of military strongman General Sani Abacha and his finance minister Anthony Ani.

Fear of putting the naira under pressure is seen by some business analysts as one of the reasons why the capital spending was held back. The other reason is a desire to make other ministries more accountable to finance.
"No inflation is nice, but what's the point of no inflation when you're dead?" asked a senior executive at a Lagos merchant bank.

Dealers on the stock exchange said the release of funds might directly benefit construction companies and others with government contracts, but cautioned that the pressure to sell which has forced the all-share index down almost five percent in the past fortnight showed no sign of letting up.
Economic crisis and political turmoil have gone side by side in Africa's most populous nation of over 100 million people since 1993 when the army annulled elections.
Abacha has restored a measure of stability, but the recession has continued to deepen.
Petrol shortages are common, despite the fact that Nigeria pumps over two million barrels per day of crude oil. Power and communications are unreliable.

Business and foreign lenders have long pushed privatisation as a means of stimulating growth, improving services and making the economy less reliant on erratic government injections of funds from its oil revenues.
"There is no doubt that privatisation is essential, not of everything, but oil refineries, power and telecommunications would all benefit," said Okeke.

The government has said it intends to privatise, but only after further study, and at its own pace -- a dissapointment for business and for Western countries already disdainful of Nigeria for alleged human rights abuses and lack of democracy.

Nigeria, with its oil and potentially huge domestic demand, is seen as a possible emerging market economy of the future. But many foreign investors are turned off by the iron grip of the military, apparently arbitrary policies and corruption.
($1 = 83 naira)
